scope: probability and measure-theory canonical dependency review

reviews.evidence: The definition takes a random variable into a measurable state space and defines its law as the pushforward probability measure, so measurable-space and pushforward-measure are direct ingredients; later PMF/PDF/CDF representations are applications.

The core defines a nonnegative measurable function whose integrals produce a probability measure on Borel sets; measurability, Lebesgue integration, and Lebesgue measure are direct hypotheses, while the RN derivative is only a later generalization.

The initial definition is the event-conditioned ratio on a probability space. Conditional expectation and random variables enter only in the later sigma-algebra-valued extension, so they should not gate the minimal core.

The theorem is stated for sigma-finite measures and absolute continuity on a measure space. Probability measures, expectation, and conditional expectation appear only in the probability application paragraph and are not theorem hypotheses.

The normal law is defined directly as a probability measure with a displayed density relative to Lebesgue measure. The RN derivative is an equivalent abstraction, not needed to construct this core example.
The interval uniform law is specified by its constant Lebesgue density. The RN derivative is not needed for the definition and was only redundant representation metadata.

The theorem assumes iid variables with finite expectation and variance. Chebyshev is mentioned as one proof route and the probability space is already supplied by the variables; neither belongs in the theorem's dependency boundary.
The statement assumes iid variables and integrability and concludes almost-sure convergence. The weak law is a later comparison, so it is not a prerequisite for the strong-law statement.

The distance is a supremum over measurable events for two probability measures on one measurable space; the prior measurable-set-only mapping omitted the objects being compared and their ambient space.

The derivative is an almost-everywhere unique measurable function on a measurable space representing one measure relative to another. Those measurable-space, measurability, measurable-set, and a.e. notions are direct; existence is supplied separately by the theorem.

Segal's definition explicitly places the isonormal map and its jointly Gaussian random variables on an auxiliary probability space; Hilbert space and linear-map prerequisites alone omitted two defining ingredients.

Fatou's statement quantifies over a sequence of nonnegative measurable functions and integrates their pointwise liminf. The sequence foundation is direct; monotone and dominated convergence are related later theorems, not prerequisites.

The core Beppo Levi statement requires a measure space, a sequence of nonnegative measurable functions, and nonnegative/Lebesgue integration. Almost-everywhere equality and null-set arguments are confined to the later variant paragraph.
